content: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the colon, characterized by alternating periods of active disease and symptom-free remission. There is limited evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of complementary or alternative medicines for managing UC. Curcumin, a compound with anti-inflammatory properties, has been utilized in various chronic inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, esophagitis, and post-surgical inflammation. However, its efficacy in maintaining remission in UC has not been systematically evaluated. The primary aim of this study was to systematically assess the efficacy and safety of curcumin for maintaining remission in UC. A comprehensive literature search was conducted on July 11, 2012, using databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the Cochrane Inflammatory Bowel Disease Specialized Trial Register. Additionally, proceedings from major gastroenterology conferences and references from published articles were reviewed to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated curcumin for maintaining remission in UC. Participants of any age who were in remission at the time of recruitment were included, and co-interventions were permitted. Two independent authors extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the included studies using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Data analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan 5.1), with relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) with 95% CI calculated for continuous outcomes. Only one trial, involving 89 patients, met the inclusion criteria. In this trial, 45 patients were randomized to receive curcumin, while 44 patients received a placebo. All participants were also treated with either sulfasalazine or mesalamine. The study was assessed as having a low risk of bias. Curcumin was administered orally at a dose of 2 g/day for six months. At the six-month mark, fewer patients in the curcumin group experienced a relapse compared to the placebo group. Specifically, 4% of patients in the curcumin group relapsed, compared to 18% in the placebo group (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.09; P = 0.06). However, this difference was not statistically significant. At 12 months, relapse rates were also not significantly different, with 22% of curcumin patients relapsing compared to 32% of placebo patients (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.40; P = 0.31). A total of nine adverse events were reported in seven patients. These adverse events included sensations of abdominal bloating, nausea, transient hypertension, and a temporary increase in stool frequency. The study did not specify which treatment groups the patients experiencing adverse events belonged to. The clinical activity index (CAI) at six months was significantly lower in the curcumin group compared to the placebo group (1.0 ± 2.0 versus 2.2 ± 2.3; MD -1.20, 95% CI -2.14 to -0.26). Similarly, the endoscopic index (EI) at six months was significantly lower in the curcumin group than in the placebo group (0.8 ± 0.6 versus 1.6 ± 1.6; MD -0.80, 95% CI -1.33 to -0.27). In conclusion, curcumin appears to be a safe and potentially effective adjunctive therapy for maintaining remission in quiescent UC when used alongside mesalamine or sulfasalazine. However, further research, particularly large-scale, methodologically rigorous randomized controlled trials, is necessary to confirm the potential benefits of curcumin in this context.
